title: 08. Files & Errors: Reading & Writing Text Files
summary: Key Rule: write() does NOT add \n automatically. You must add it yourself! print() adds \n automatically.

sections.title: Concept Explanation (Junior Developer Style)
sections.body:
### Reading Methods:

```
read()        → Read ENTIRE file as ONE big string
readline()    → Read ONE line at a time (includes \n)
readlines()   → Read ALL lines into a LIST
for line in f → Read line by line (BEST for large files!)
```

### Writing Methods:

```
write(str)        → Write a string (NO automatic newline!)
writelines(list)  → Write list of strings (NO automatic newlines!)
print(..., file=f)→ Write with automatic newline
```

> 🧠 **Key Rule**: `write()` does NOT add `\n` automatically. You must add it yourself! `print()` adds `\n` automatically.

sections.title: 5 Examples
sections.body:
```python
# ── Example 1: All reading methods compared ───────────────────────────
# Create a sample file
sample_content = """Line 1: Hello World
Line 2: Python File Handling
Line 3: Reading Methods
Line 4: Interview Preparation
Line 5: Last Line
"""

with open("sample.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(sample_content)

print("="*50)
print("METHOD 1: read() — entire file as string")
print("="*50)
with open("sample.txt", "r") as f:
    content = f.read()
print(repr(content[:50]))   # shows \n characters
print(f"Type: {type(content)}, Length: {len(content)} chars")

print("\n" + "="*50)
print("METHOD 2: readline() — one line at a time")
print("="*50)
with open("sample.txt", "r") as f:
    line1 = f.readline()    # reads including \n
    line2 = f.readline()    # reads next line
    line3 = f.readline()
print(f"Line 1: {repr(line1)}")
print(f"Line 2: {repr(line2)}")

print("\n" + "="*50)
print("METHOD 3: readlines() — all lines as list")
print("="*50)
with open("sample.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()   # list of strings with \n
print(f"Type: {type(lines)}, Count: {len(lines)}")
print(f"First: {repr(lines[0])}")
print(f"Last:  {repr(lines[-1])}")

print("\n" + "="*50)
print("METHOD 4: for loop — BEST for large files")
print("="*50)
with open("sample.txt", "r") as f:
    for i, line in enumerate(f, 1):
        print(f"  Line {i}: {line.rstrip()}")  # rstrip() removes \n
```

```python
# ── Example 2: seek() and tell() — file pointer control ───────────────
with open("sample.txt", "r") as f:
    print(f"Start position: {f.tell()}")       # 0

    # Read first line
    line1 = f.readline()
    print(f"After readline: {f.tell()}")       # position after line 1

    # Read a few chars
    chars = f.read(10)
    print(f"After read(10): {f.tell()}")       # moved forward 10

    # Go back to beginning
    f.seek(0)
    print(f"After seek(0):  {f.tell()}")       # back to 0

    # Read entire file
    all_content = f.read()

    # Go to end using seek
    f.seek(0, 2)  # 0 bytes from end
    print(f"At end:         {f.tell()}")       # total file size

    # Read last 20 bytes
    f.seek(-20, 2)  # 20 bytes before end
    last_part = f.read()
    print(f"Last 20 chars: {repr(last_part)}")
```

```python
# ── Example 3: All writing methods compared ───────────────────────────
# write() — no automatic newline!
with open("write_demo.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Line 1")           # NO \n — next write continues here
    f.write(" continued\n")     # NOW newline
    f.write("Line 2\n")
    f.write("Line 3\n")

# writelines() — writes list items, NO automatic newlines
lines = ["Apple\n", "Banana\n", "Cherry\n"]  # must include \n!
with open("write_demo.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.writelines(lines)         # writes all items, no separator added

# print() to file — automatic newline
with open("write_demo.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print("Added with print()", file=f)     # adds \n automatically
    print("Line 2 via print", file=f)       # adds \n automatically
    print("Sep demo", end=" | ", file=f)    # custom end
    print("Next part", file=f)

print("=== File contents ===")
with open("write_demo.txt", "r") as f:
    print(f.read())

import os
os.remove("write_demo.txt")
```

```python
# ── Example 4: Append mode vs Write mode ──────────────────────────────
import os

filename = "append_demo.txt"

# First write — creates file
with open(filename, "w") as f:
    f.write("Original line 1\n")
    f.write("Original line 2\n")

print("After initial write:")
print(open(filename).read())

# 'a' mode — ADDS to end, keeps existing content
with open(filename, "a") as f:
    f.write("Appended line 3\n")
    f.write("Appended line 4\n")

print("After append:")
print(open(filename).read())

# 'w' mode again — DELETES everything!
with open(filename, "w") as f:
    f.write("OVERWROTE all previous content!\n")

print("After write (overwrote):")
print(open(filename).read())

os.remove(filename)
```

```python
# ── Example 5: Real world — reading and processing a config file ───────
import os

# Create a config file
config_content = """# Server Configuration File
# Lines starting with # are comments

HOST=localhost
PORT=8080
DATABASE=myapp_db
DEBUG=True
MAX_CONNECTIONS=100
LOG_LEVEL=INFO
SECRET_KEY=my-super-secret-key-2024
"""

with open("server.conf", "w") as f:
    f.write(config_content)

def parse_config_file(filepath):
    """Parse simple KEY=VALUE config file"""
    config = {}

    with open(filepath, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line_num, line in enumerate(f, 1):
            # Strip whitespace
            line = line.strip()

            # Skip empty lines and comments
            if not line or line.startswith("#"):
                continue

            # Parse KEY=VALUE
            if "=" not in line:
                print(f"⚠️  Line {line_num}: Invalid format: {line}")
                continue

            key, _, value = line.partition("=")
            key   = key.strip()
            value = value.strip()

            # Type conversion
            if value.lower() == "true":
                value = True
            elif value.lower() == "false":
                value = False
            elif value.isdigit():
                value = int(value)

            config[key] = value

    return config

config = parse_config_file("server.conf")
print("Parsed config:")
for key, value in config.items():
    print(f"  {key:<20}: {value!r:>30}  ({type(value).__name__})")

os.remove("server.conf")
```

quiz.question: What is the difference between read(), readline(), and readlines()?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > Text mode ('r', 'w'): Python automatically handles encoding/decoding and newline translation (\n on Unix, \r\n on Windows).
5-Year Exp Answer: > > > > JSONDecodeError subclasses ValueError.
5-Year Exp Answer: > There are 8 core modes: 'r' (read-only, default), 'w' (write, creates/overwrites), 'a' (append, preserves content), 'x' (exclusive create, fails if…
5-Year Exp Answer: > read() reads the entire file as one string — loads everything into memory. readline() reads one line at a time — returns an empty string at EOF.…
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: read() reads the entire file as one string — loads everything into memory. readline() reads one line at a time — returns an empty string at EOF. readlines() reads all lines into a list — each element includes \n. For small files (< 100MB), any works.

quiz.question: Why does write() not add a newline automatically?
options: S1. Your application processes user-uploaded files.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Text mode ('r', 'w'): Python automatically handles encoding/decoding and newline translation (\n on Unix, \r\n on Windows).
5-Year Exp Answer: > The csv module handles its own newline processing internally.
5-Year Exp Answer: > By design — Python gives you control over exactly what's written. write() writes exactly what you pass.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: By design — Python gives you control over exactly what's written. write() writes exactly what you pass. If it added \n automatically, you couldn't write partial lines or binary-like text. The trade-off: you must always remember to add \n.

options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > All file exceptions inherit from OSError (also aliased as IOError for backwards compatibility).
5-Year Exp Answer: > os.remove() deletes a single file only — raises IsADirectoryError on directories. os.rmdir() deletes an empty directory — raises OSError if…
5-Year Exp Answer: > Text mode ('r', 'w'): Python automatically handles encoding/decoding and newline translation (\n on Unix, \r\n on Windows).
5-Year Exp Answer: > 'w' (write) TRUNCATES the file to zero length first — any existing content is GONE. 'a' (append) keeps existing content and writes new data at the…
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: 'w' (write) TRUNCATES the file to zero length first — any existing content is GONE. 'a' (append) keeps existing content and writes new data at the END. Critical production concern: using 'w' when you meant 'a' is a data loss bug. Real scenario: log files must ALWAYS use 'a' — using 'w' would erase all previous logs on every server restart.

5-Year Exp Answer: > Use f.read(size) which reads up to size bytes: > > > > Why: (1) Memory efficiency — 10GB file, 8KB chunks = constant ~8KB memory.

quiz.question: What happens if you call read() twice on the same file object?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > > > > Real-world use: QUOTE_ALL for user data that might contain commas/quotes.
5-Year Exp Answer: > f.tell() returns the current byte position of the file pointer. f.seek(offset, whence) moves the pointer. whence=0 (default) — from beginning,…
5-Year Exp Answer: > errno provides named constants for OS error numbers. e.errno on an OSError gives you the numeric error code.
5-Year Exp Answer: > The second read() returns an empty string because the file pointer is already at the end of file (EOF).
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: The second read() returns an empty string because the file pointer is already at the end of file (EOF). The file pointer advances as you read. To read again: call f.seek(0) to go back to the beginning.
